# Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta (MN 31 (PTS MN i 205))

**ID:** MN 31 (PTS MN i 205)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Shorter Discourse at Gosiṅga
**PTS:** MN i 205
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn31
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷagosinga Sutta* (MN 31, PTS MN i 205) recounts the Buddha's visit to the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Wood (*Gosiṅgasālavanadāya*) while residing at the Giñjakāvasatha in Nātika [Galasek 2016]. Upon arrival, a park keeper who does not recognize the Buddha tries to turn him away so as not to disturb three resident clan-sons, until Anuruddha intervenes to welcome their teacher [Galasek 2016]. The three monastics dwelling together in the grove are Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila [Buddhist Virtues 2011; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. The Buddha inquires about their welfare and how they manage to live in perfect harmony [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Anuruddha explains that although they are different in body, they are of one mind, treating one another with loving-kindness in deeds, words, and thoughts, "blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes" [Buddhist Virtues 2011; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. They share practical monastic chores and observe harmonious, appropriate silence, which the Buddha commends as an adornment to the grove [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2010; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. When pressed on their meditative progress, Anuruddha reveals their mastery of the nine successive meditative abidings (*anupubbavihāra*)—the four *jhāna*s, the four immaterial attainments, and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodha*)—having surmounted each stage until attaining the destruction of the taints [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2016; Polak 2011].

Curated parallels include a Sarvāstivāda recension in the Chinese *Madhyamāgama* (MĀ 185), an *Ekottarikāgama* discourse (EĀ 24.8), a Sanskrit fragment (SHT sutta75), and closely related narratives in the Pali Vinaya (*Kosambakakkhandhaka*, Kd 10) and the *Upakkilesa Sutta* (MN 128) [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. A Gāndhārī version is preserved among the Senior collection manuscripts [Buswell 2004]. Text-reuse computation demonstrates extensive shared material with Kd 10 (§3.2–9.9) and MN 128 (§3.2–10.2), along with alignments across MĀ, EĀ, and the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya (*Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Śayanāsanavastu*) [DharmaNexus]. While MN 128 depicts the trio striving at an earlier stage of training, MN 31 portrays them as fully accomplished arahants [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995].
